frameworks.name: Per-Asset Pricing over Tiered Ladders
frameworks.definition: For ultra-bespoke high-net-worth service businesses, pricing by the asset being worked on (yacht, plane, house) with a small annual continuity retainer outperforms complex multi-tier commitment ladders because it matches client desire for flexibility and speed.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that for ultra-bespoke service businesses targeting ultra-high-net-worth clients, a tiered pricing ladder only works when higher tiers are priced at roughly 5x the lower tier; if the price difference between tiers is only 20-25% (e.g., $80/sq ft vs $100/sq ft), the tiers are too undifferentiated to justify a commitment ladder and the structure collapses.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: If the price difference between tiers is small, prospects perceive no meaningful value gap between commitments and will default to the lower tier or reject the ladder entirely rather than escalating.

numbers.axis: price multiple between adjacent tiers in a commitment ladder

bounded_by: Applies to bespoke high-touch luxury services; mass-market tiered SaaS products operate differently

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that ultra-high-net-worth clients prioritize flexibility, speed, and certainty of outcome over multi-year commitment structures; 10- to 15-year contract commitments feel restrictive to this demographic and create friction rather than loyalty.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Wealthy clients have optionality by definition; locking them into long commitments removes the optionality they pay a premium to preserve, making the long-term structure a liability rather than a feature.
bounded_by: May not apply to institutional clients (family offices) who do engage in long-term vendor relationships for operational simplicity

claims.text: Alex Hormozi advises that for ultra-high-net-worth home services, an annual continuity retainer should be priced as a rounding error relative to the project cost (e.g., a $500/year maintenance plan on a $100,000 project, roughly 0.5%) because the retainer's economic value is not the fee itself but the guaranteed annual access it provides to a wealthy household that will generate ongoing project revenue.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: client has ongoing acquisition of assets (homes, yachts, planes)
claims.mechanism: An annual visit positions the provider as an established vendor; once inside a wealthy household in that trusted-vendor role, the client will voluntarily reveal upcoming projects and the provider can scope and price additional work, generating compounding revenue beyond the retainer fee itself.

numbers.axis: annual retainer as percentage of original project cost

bounded_by: Strategy assumes client continues accumulating assets; does not apply to one-time buyers with no ongoing real estate or asset portfolio

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that in luxury bespoke service businesses, small maintenance or follow-on jobs should not be avoided because small jobs generate access to large jobs; for ultra-high-net-worth clients who regularly purchase homes, yachts, and planes, a small renovation in an off-year maintains the relationship and top-of-mind position that leads to large project mandates.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.speaker_term: the small jobs get the big jobs
conditions: clients who regularly acquire new assets
claims.mechanism: Wealthy clients purchase new homes, yachts, or planes on a recurring cadence; a provider who remains visible and trusted via small engagements in off-years is the automatic first call for large projects, whereas a provider who only accepts large mandates loses continuity and top-of-mind status.
bounded_by: Does not apply when small jobs are structurally unprofitable for the provider or require significant overhead without margin

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that for ultra-bespoke luxury services, per-square-foot pricing (e.g., $80 or $100 per square foot) is not a meaningful signal to ultra-high-net-worth buyers or family office CEOs; such buyers will simply do the math on total project cost and evaluate the proposal on outcome quality and professional presentation, not the unit rate.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: ultra-high-net-worth buyer or family office CEO
bespoke interior design / wellness advisory service
claims.mechanism: Wealthy institutional buyers are outcome-oriented and relationship-driven; they compare vendors on perceived quality, reputation, and fit rather than on unit-price arithmetic, so a per-square-foot figure carries no comparative anchor and functions only as a back-calculation tool for total cost.
bounded_by: Per-square-foot pricing is appropriate as an internal estimation tool; it can be shared as a cost-estimate methodology but should not be the primary price signal in client-facing positioning

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for ultra-high-net-worth buyers who are not price-shopping but seeking the best outcome, winning proposals are decided by perceived professionalism, aesthetic quality, and brand finishes rather than by price competitiveness; price is secondary when the buyer has already been referred or is self-selecting into a premium vendor.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Buyers who are not price-sensitive are comparing perceived value signals (aesthetics, presentation, referral credibility) rather than unit cost; a more polished professional presentation wins independent of the price, because the buyer is already committed to spending what it takes.
bounded_by: Does not apply when three competing bids are mandated by a family office procurement process at similar price levels

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends that ultra-high-net-worth service businesses set a floor qualification criterion publicly (e.g., $20M+ estate minimum) rather than leading with per-unit pricing, because the stated minimum pre-qualifies prospects and causes them to arrive on calls already expecting a high total price without explicit price anchoring.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Stating a minimum estate or asset threshold in positioning filters unqualified prospects and simultaneously signals exclusivity; prospects who pass the filter self-assess as qualified and assume the price will be significant, reducing price-shock resistance in the sales conversation.

numbers.axis: minimum estate value as public qualification threshold

bounded_by: May deter borderline prospects who could grow into the client profile; requires the provider to actually enforce the floor

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that for ultra-bespoke luxury service businesses, pricing should be determined per-asset (house, yacht, plane, office) rather than by a commitment-tier ladder; the asset-level pricing naturally scales with the value of each asset, producing appropriate revenue without requiring clients to pre-commit to a service tier.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: clients with multiple asset types (homes, yachts, planes)
claims.mechanism: Asset-level pricing preserves client flexibility while allowing fees to scale naturally with project value; a yacht, jet, and home each carry inherent value signals that anchor price expectations without requiring a multi-year commitment ladder that the client resists.
bounded_by: Requires provider to scope and price each asset type separately; not suitable for standardized service packages

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for bespoke luxury services, simplifying pricing to a single round number (e.g., $100 per square foot vs. $80) is preferable because clients can do the mental arithmetic instantly; pricing clarity and simplicity reduce friction in the initial engagement, whereas differentiated fractional rates add cognitive load without adding value.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: sophisticated buyer who will self-calculate total cost
claims.mechanism: Simple round numbers allow instant mental calculation; complex fractional pricing creates unnecessary friction and signals operational immaturity rather than premium confidence.

examples.text: In the conversation, Alex Hormozi illustrates the continuity retainer model using a home services analogy: if a provider sells a $100,000 project, they add a $500/year maintenance plan framed as insurance — the provider comes by once a year to confirm everything is working correctly. The economic purpose of this visit is not the $500 fee but the guaranteed annual access: once inside a wealthy client's home as an established vendor, the client will reveal upcoming projects (renovations, new properties, new acquisitions) and the provider can scope additional work on the spot. This example demonstrates the mechanism by which a nominally de minimis retainer generates recurring large-project revenue from a compounding relationship.

Sarah (the interior design business owner) describes her existing three-tier ladder: Tier 1 at $80/sq ft for project-based home renovations (20-year established service), Tier 2 at $100/sq ft for a 7-10 year commitment across an entire real estate portfolio with locked rates and sequencing strategy, and Tier 3 at $100/sq ft plus a $200,000 annual stewardship retainer for whole-ecosystem advisory (yacht, plane, offices, curated annual experiences, 15-year roadmap, annual council reviews). Alex Hormozi responds that the Tier 2 and Tier 3 structures caused him to squint because the price difference between tiers was too small (~25%) to justify the escalating commitment level, and the long multi-year lock-in runs against ultra-high-net-worth client preferences for flexibility. This example concretely illustrates the failure mode of insufficient price differentiation in a commitment ladder and the mismatch between long-term commitment structure and wealthy-client psychology.

practices.text: When building a continuity retainer for a luxury service business, frame the annual visit as insurance rather than maintenance; call it a stewardship review or strategic review, not a maintenance plan, to match the premium brand positioning.

For bespoke ultra-high-net-worth services, avoid publishing per-unit pricing (e.g., per square foot) as the primary client-facing price signal; use it internally for estimation and share it only as a calculation methodology on client calls when needed to set expectations.

At the end of each annual continuity visit to a wealthy client, proactively ask what else they have in the pipeline of asset acquisition so you can identify and scope upcoming projects before other vendors are invited.

When advising a bespoke service founder on pricing, replace a multi-tier commitment ladder with per-asset pricing plus a small continuity retainer if the core service is already highly bespoke and clients have diverse asset types.
